terminal_teaching.prerequisite_note: No Linux experience needed. Type one command in the terminal input and press Enter or Run. These commands affect only the lesson’s simulated files.

concepts.title: Know where you are
concepts.text: A directory is a folder. pwd prints your current folder; ls lists its visible names. Commands and names are case-sensitive. A command often finishes without printing anything when it succeeds.

concepts.title: Move through folders
concepts.text: cd NAME enters a folder. A path names a location: /home/alex is absolute, starting at the simulated root /. A relative path starts where you are. A slash joins folder names; .. means the parent folder. cd alone returns home.

concepts.title: Read, then copy
concepts.text: cat FILE prints a text file. cp SOURCE DESTINATION makes a separate copy and leaves the source in place. Use a space between the command and each name. Type in the input below the transcript, not in its printed output.

terminal_teaching.inputs: This practice home contains a workshop folder and its welcome.txt. Run each example command in order. The assignment uses a different project.
terminal_teaching.try_change: After copying, run ls and cat copied.txt. Then try cd .. followed by pwd.

concepts.title: Keep a name together
concepts.text: Spaces normally separate command arguments. Single quotes around a name keep its spaces together: cat 'meeting agenda.txt' reads one file. Double quotes also work for these literal paths; variable expansion is not part of this terminal.

concepts.title: Create a folder
concepts.text: mkdir PATH creates one directory whose parent already exists. cp SOURCE DIRECTORY keeps the source name inside that directory; cp SOURCE DIRECTORY/NEWNAME chooses a new name. Existing destination files can be overwritten, so inspect first.

concepts.title: Copy or move?
concepts.text: cp makes a second file. mv changes a file’s name or location; its old name disappears. Both take a source and destination. A destination folder keeps the source base name. An existing destination file is replaced, so check it before acting.

concepts.title: Verify the result
concepts.text: Use ls on both folders, then cat the destination. A move does not require write permission on the file itself: renaming requires write and search permission on its parent folders. This exercise supplies those permissions.

concepts.title: Hidden does not mean protected
concepts.text: A name beginning with . is hidden from ordinary ls output. ls -a includes it along with . (this folder) and .. (its parent). Hidden files still need the same careful review as visible files.

concepts.title: Delete precisely
concepts.text: rm FILE removes one file, with no recycle bin in this simulation. rmdir DIRECTORY removes an empty folder and refuses one containing entries. Recursive deletion is deliberately unsupported here. Read the requirement and inspect before deleting; Reset restores this selected attempt if needed.

scenarios.title: Create a private working area by default
scenarios.summary: Set creation defaults and verify actual directory and file permissions.
scenarios.objective: Set Alex’s creation mask to 077. Create private as a directory with permission 700 and private/notes.txt as an empty file with permission 600. Keep public.txt unchanged with permission 644. Do not change /home/alex permissions.

guide.action: Inspect the starting directory and the supplied text before changing files.

guide.why: Set the mask before creating either required entry. umask alone prints the current mask.
guide.action: mkdir creates a directory; touch creates an empty ordinary file. Their base permission sets differ.

guide.title: Verify the result
guide.why: A command finishing silently is normal. Check names, contents and permissions rather than relying on the absence of an error.

scenarios.explanation: 077 removes all group and other permissions at creation. A directory needs owner search permission, so 777 with those bits blocked becomes 700; an ordinary new file starts with no execute bits, so 666 becomes 600. Existing public.txt keeps its contents and original 644 mode.
hints: Set the mask before creating either required entry. umask alone prints the current mask.
mkdir creates a directory; touch creates an empty ordinary file. Their base permission sets differ.
Use ls -ld private and ls -l private to check both levels. Changing the mask afterward does not repair already-created permissions; reset this attempt if you want a clean retry.

terminal_teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on creating folders and inspecting names. This lesson introduces permission defaults; it does not require the earlier repair lab.

concepts.title: Read the access groups
concepts.text: ls -l shows permissions in three groups: owner, group and everyone else. r means read, w means write and x means search/enter for a directory (execute for a file). A dash means that permission is absent. Alex owns these practice files.

concepts.title: Understand the numbers
concepts.text: Octal permissions combine read=4, write=2 and execute/search=1. Thus 700 gives the owner all three permissions and nobody else any; 600 gives only owner read+write. ls -ld PATH inspects the directory itself rather than its contents.

concepts.title: Choose safer creation defaults
concepts.text: umask blocks permissions on NEW entries; it does not edit existing ones. umask 077 blocks group and everyone-else access. Normal new directories start from 777, giving 700; touch creates ordinary files from 666, giving 600. touch also updates an existing entry’s time without emptying it.

terminal_teaching.inputs: The practice home is empty. Create journal and inspect its owner-only permissions.
terminal_teaching.try_change: Run umask 022, create another folder and file, and compare ls -l. Existing journal permissions stay unchanged.
